history.alt_text: Bare microbolometer detector array inside an opened thermal camera on a garage workbench, gold wire bonds visible.
history.caption: A thermal camera's actual measured resolution lives in this tiny detector array, not in the upscaled pixel count printed on the box.
history.title: Thermal Camera Detector Array vs Upscaled Resolution

style_when: the story turns on one physical thing — a part, a material, a component, a document — and what that thing costs, contains or crosses a border is the news
prompt: Extreme macro photograph on a garage workbench: a bare square microbolometer detector array exposes its fine gold grid and bond wires at lower left, the black thermal-camera housing shell folded open behind it and a blurred blank spec sheet under a corner. Hard raking daylight from the upper left glances across the sensor face, revealing tiny measured pixels. Palette of bone white, graphite, and slate grey, with textured particle-board plywood beneath. 100mm macro lens at f/2.8, razor-thin focal plane on the sensor, background falling away. Extreme asymmetry, sensor lower-left on a rule-of-thirds intersection, generous negative space top-right. Fine film grain, no people, no legible lettering.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random letters, watermarks, logo, UI, legible words, numbers, captions, labels, typography
rationale: Editorial macro locks the eye on the exact component where the deception lives: the tiny detector array versus the box's inflated resolution. A raking macro shot turns an abstract spec dispute into a tactile piece of hardware.
cue: detector row in its spec table counts measured ones
subject: a bare microbolometer detector array in an opened thermal camera
core_thesis: The resolution on a thermal camera's box counts drawn pixels; the detector row in its spec table counts measured ones, and only the second number says what the camera can see.
core_conflict: marketed interpolated resolution vs native detector pixel count — upscaled 512×384 imagery masquerading as measured detail while the true 256×192 array remains the only real temperature data
composition: extreme asymmetry, detector chip lower-left on a rule-of-thirds intersection, trailing ribbon cable receding toward top-right
alt_text: Thermal Camera 10X Resolution Illusion. Bare microbolometer detector array inside an opened thermal camera on a garage workbench, gold wire
caption: Thermal Camera 10X Resolution Illusion: The advertised 512×384 is drawn, not measured; the detector grid is the real resolution.
title: Thermal Camera 10X Resolution Illusion

review.depicts: A bare ceramic-packaged chip with a central square die and gold-plated contact traces lies on a strand-board surface in the lower-left, with an empty black plastic camera-like housing behind and to the left and a white sheet of paper extending toward the upper right.
review.reason: The frame shows the article's core object — a bare chip die standing in for the detector array whose measured pixels are the story — though it reads more as a generic processor package than a microbolometer and lacks the ordered ribbon cable.
